records.our_prose: Strawberry feeding is nitrogen-driven and timed to the planting model. In the first year, apply a total of about 0.5 to 0.8 ounces of actual nitrogen per 10 feet of row, split across the season: a small dose one to two weeks after planting, a second about a month later, and a third roughly two months after planting. On established June-bearing beds, do not feed in spring; spring nitrogen drives leaf growth, not fruit, and a dense canopy traps moisture and promotes gray mold. Instead, fertilize once at renovation, just after harvest, to build the flower buds for next year. Established day-neutral and everbearing plants, which fruit all season, take the same total split into monthly doses through summer with an optional August feeding. On sandy soil, divide every rate into more frequent, lighter applications.

records.our_prose: The interior valley grows strawberries as a spring-cropping annual rather than a perennial bed, since summer heat and soilborne disease pressure cut productive life to one or two seasons. Short-day varieties planted in August do most of their fruiting the following spring, with harvest running from mid-April through mid-June and heaviest picking in May and June. Plants set in August may put out a small flush of blossoms the first fall, but removing those fall blossoms channels energy into crown development and produces a heavier spring crop. Replace the bed with fresh nursery stock every two to three years as heat and disease pressure accumulate. White mulch over the bed in summer keeps the soil cooler and reduces fruit burn once temperatures climb above 90°F.

records.our_prose: In peninsular Florida (zones 10 and 11), strawberries are a winter crop, not a bed that comes back for years. Plant transplants in the fall, from late September to early November, on raised beds covered with plastic so the roots drain and the berries stay clean. You will get flowers starting around November and berries in waves from late fall into April or May. When hot, wet summer weather returns, pull the plants out and plant fresh ones the next fall, because young plants make the best fruit. In zone 10 a rare cold night can hurt the flowers, so keep a frost cloth ready to cover the bed; zone 11 does not freeze. Try not to plant where strawberries, tomatoes, peppers, or eggplant grew in the last couple of years, to avoid soil diseases.

records.our_prose: Florida is the winter strawberry capital, and in peninsular Florida (zones 10 and 11) strawberries are grown as a winter annual, not a perennial bed. Florida's fall, winter, and spring supply the cool temperatures (about 50°F to 80°F) and short days needed for flowering and fruit, while summer heat and rain exhaust the planting. Set bare-root or plug transplants in fall, from late September to early November (mid to late October in central and west-central Florida), on raised beds covered with black plastic mulch for drainage and clean fruit. Expect flowering from November and fruit in two or three cycles from late fall into April or May, then pull and discard the plants; the highest-quality fruit comes from young plants, so replant fresh each fall. Zone 10 can see a rare freeze that nips open blossoms, so keep frost cloth handy during bloom; zone 11 is frost-free. Rotate away from beds that grew strawberries, tomatoes, peppers, or eggplant in the past two to three years to limit soilborne disease.

records.our_prose: In the north (zones 3 to 7), strawberries are a perennial: you plant them once and the same bed comes back and fruits for several years. Plant the small brown dormant crowns in early spring, as soon as you can dig the soil, even if frost is still possible. June-bearing kinds give one big batch of berries in late spring or early summer, about a month after they bloom, then grow runners that root into new plants and fill the row. After the berries finish, cut the leaves back and thin the plants to keep the bed healthy, and start a fresh bed every three or four years. In zone 3, cover plants with straw over winter for protection; berries are most reliable from zone 4 and warmer.

records.our_prose: Across the maritime Northwest, strawberries are grown as a perennial matted-row bed, and June-bearing types are a genuine regional strength: WSU Clallam County Extension names Benton, Hood, Rainier, Puget Reliance, Puget Summer, Sweet Sunrise, Shuksan, and Tillamook as the recommended maritime cultivars, cropping June into July. Set dormant bare-root crowns about two weeks before the last frost, as soon as the soil can be worked, and renovate the bed within about a week of the last picking (mow the leaves, narrow the row, fertilize). Open blossoms are damaged at 30°F, so cover the bed on a forecast frosty night during May bloom. Zone 8 sits right at this crop's cold edge for the crown; mulch with straw once the ground freezes and pull it back in spring. Zone 9's milder winter floor sits comfortably above that edge.

records.our_prose: In the Rio Grande Valley, strawberries are a winter crop you grow and then replace, not a bed that lives for years. Plant in fall, pick berries in late winter and early spring, then pull the plants out when summer heat arrives and plant new ones the next fall. Raised beds covered with plastic keep the roots drained and the berries clean.

records.our_prose: Renovation is a once-a-year tidy-up for June-bearing strawberries, done a week or two after the last berries are picked. Mow or cut the old leaves down to about 2 inches above the crowns (the thick stems at soil level), being careful not to cut into the crowns. Rake away the cut leaves, narrow the row back to about a hand's width by removing plants from the edges, then feed and water so the plants put out fresh leaves before winter. Skip this for day-neutral and everbearing types, since they are still making fruit in late summer.

records.our_prose: Renovation applies to June-bearing matted rows. Do it within a week or two of picking the final berries, while the plants still have time to regrow before fall. Mow or shear the old leaves to roughly 2 inches above the crowns without cutting into the crowns themselves, rake out the debris to cut next spring's fruit rot, narrow the row back to about 10 to 12 inches by tilling or hoeing the edges, then fertilize and water to push fresh leaf and runner growth. Leave day-neutral and everbearing plants alone, since they are still fruiting in late summer.

records.our_prose: Strawberries want a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam with steady but not excessive moisture. The roots are shallow and fibrous, so they suffocate in soil that stays waterlogged for more than a day or two, and root rots follow. On heavy or slow-draining ground, plant into a raised bed or mounded row about 12 inches high so water drains away from the crowns. Work 1 to 2 inches of compost or aged organic matter into the bed before planting to lift organic matter above 3 percent.

records.our_prose: Strawberries want a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam rich in organic matter. Because the roots are shallow and rot in waterlogged soil, plant into a raised bed or mounded row about 12 inches high on heavy or slow-draining ground. Work 1 to 2 inches of compost into the bed before planting and adjust pH to 5.6 to 6.5 a season ahead, since sulfur or lime take months to act. Avoid ground that recently grew tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries, which leave Verticillium wilt in the soil.

records.our_prose: There is no hardening-off step for strawberries. You plant them either as dormant bare-root crowns, which look like a clump of roots with a small bud, or as small potted plants from a garden center. records.our_prose: There are three kinds of strawberries, and picking the right one matters more than picking a fancy variety. June-bearing types give you one big harvest over about four weeks in late spring or early summer, perfect if you want a pile of berries at once for jam or the freezer. They spread by sending out runners that fill in a wide row, and they give their first real crop the year after you plant them. Day-neutral types fruit a little at a time from late spring all the way to fall, give berries the first year, and stay compact, so they are the best choice for pots and small raised beds. Everbearing types fall in between, with one crop in early summer and another in late summer. This guide is built around the June-bearing kind grown in a wide row, since that is how most home gardeners grow strawberries, and it points out along the way where day-neutrals are handled differently. In mild coastal areas with gentle winters, day-neutral plants can give berries through much of the year, and gardeners there often plant fresh ones each year instead of keeping a bed for years.

records.our_prose: Strawberries come in three types, and the choice shapes your whole season. June-bearing cultivars set flower buds in the short days of fall and deliver one concentrated crop over about four weeks in late spring or early summer; they throw the most runners, so they suit a matted row and give a large flush ideal for freezing and jam. Their first real crop comes the season after planting. Day-neutral cultivars flower regardless of day length whenever temperatures sit between about 40 and 90°F, so they fruit from late spring through fall, bear in their first season, and throw few runners, which makes them the pick for containers, raised beds, and a steady supply of fresh berries. Everbearing cultivars give two lighter crops, one in early summer and one in late summer, and are generally less productive than day-neutrals. This guide follows the June-bearing matted-row model because it is the backbone of US backyard strawberry growing; the day-neutral notes throughout tell you where the care diverges. In mild-winter coastal regions, day-neutral plantings can fruit across much of the year and are often grown as a fall-set annual rather than a long-lived bed, which is why the warm-region notes treat them differently from the cold-region matted row.
